narrative:
The model estimated a 94% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt, and because that risk was high, your law school application was denied. This does not mean you cannot become a lawyer; it means this application, as presented, did not overcome the model’s concern about bar-exam readiness.

The strongest reason was your third-year class ranking. You were in the lowest decile, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile. That gap strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. Your first-year class ranking was the next most influential factor: you were also in the lowest decile there, compared with an accepted-student average near the sixth decile, which again pushed toward failure. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.10 was slightly below the accepted average of 3.23. This factor modestly pushed toward passing, but it was not strong enough to offset the two class-rank signals.

To improve future applications, focus on evidence that you can handle bar-level work: raise your LSAT if possible, complete additional rigorous coursework or a post-baccalaureate/master’s program with strong grades, and meet with admissions advisers to explain your trajectory. Consider delaying applications until you can show sustained academic improvement and bar-readiness, and prepare early for the bar exam.
